donts: Don't mix the two palettes, or put a platform component on a landing page.
Don't shadow a panel, card, button or field. Shadows belong to things sitting on the paper – pucks, stickers, tape, reels.
Don't set text a participant must read in line-strong, teal, gold-deep, orange-deep, coral or sky-deep on cream, or white on sky, teal, orange or teal-grey – all below 4.5:1 (see Measured contrast).
Don't put .sketch on an <input>, <select> or <textarea>; it cannot render there.
Don't trust --color-hl-yellow*: those variables hold blues.
Don't set Masterpiece in bold, or use it for anything but the wordmark.
Don't apply the wobble filter to anything containing text.
Don't nest panels, and don't reach for a panel when the content is a path, a feed or a form.
Don't stack chips as a page's structure; a fact that needs no emphasis goes in the quiet hand-text line.
Don't use a Unicode glyph as an icon. Icons are drawn SVG on a 24px grid at a 1.8px round stroke.
dos: Do pick the world first. A platform screen uses the platform palette, Plus Jakarta, drawn edges and 16px panels; a landing section uses ink, Ubuntu, Open Sans and square plates.
Do draw platform borders with .sketch / .sketch-2 / .sketch-3 and vary them between neighbouring panels.
Do keep a disabled control in place and say why next to it; never hide a control because it can't be used right now.
Do let a puck's colour say its state, and say the rest in the bubble that hangs above it.
Do give every focusable surface the ring: magenta, 3px, 3px offset on the platform; accent, 3px, 2px offset in the staff console.
Do keep one size per text role on a screen: asides 0.84rem, body 0.9rem, timeline titles 0.95rem.
Do put the content first when the platform collapses; below lg the chrome moves to a header and a bottom tab bar.
keyCharacteristics: Two grounds, never mixed: #31222c ink for the landing, #fcf7f7 warm paper for the platform, with a faint 28px graph-paper tooth so the cream reads as paper rather than dimmed white.
The landing is flat and mostly square; the platform has drawn edges, pucks that sit on a rim, and a few stickers lifted off the page.

The platform's borders are drawn, not declared: .sketch puts a wobbling marker outline on a pseudo-element so the line never touches the content it frames, and .torn applies the same displacement to a filled shape – which is how the week banners and page signs get their torn-tape edge.
Its checkpoint token is the .puck: a rim disc offset beneath a face disc, an ambient shadow under both, and a press that sinks the face onto the rim.
The platform's primary structure is a progress path, not a dashboard of cards.
Illustration is the programme's own: a cast of fox and gato characters and five theme paintings, all die-cut stickers with a pale outline.
Text is navy and navy-soft, never neutral grey; the hand face writes the asides in the margin.
narrative.northStar: Two worlds: "The Production Line" (landing) and "The Field Notebook" (platform)
narrative.overview:
Half Life runs two visual worlds on purpose, and the split is the first thing to understand before writing any screen. The marketing site sells a ten-week hardware programme to teenagers who have never soldered anything. The platform is where those same teenagers then work, for ten weeks, most days. A world that serves the first badly serves the second, so they were never merged.

There is a third, which is not a world so much as a back room: the staff console under (ops) – admin and review – carries the platform's earlier design system in ops.css, kept rather than half-translated when the participant platform was rebuilt from the comp. In the CSS its tokens are plain --color-* names; this document prefixes them ops- so they cannot be mistaken for the platform's. It redefines names the platform also uses (ink, teal, mint, magenta), so the stylesheet scopes them to .ops-root, the wrapper the console renders inside: on :root they would quietly repaint the trail after a navigation. The stylesheet is plain CSS over the platform's Tailwind, not a second copy of it. The phone handoff page is a third root layout – public by design, so it cannot sit under the session-gated shell – but it is drawn in the platform's world rather than the console's: the same stylesheet, fonts and filter definitions.

A ten-week hardware production line, drawn as the line itself. The page reads like control-panel silkscreen laid over a workshop: flat plates, square-cut bands, no shadows, and a thick band that physically welds each stage of the programme to the next. The ground is ink and the informational plates are paper, because this is read on a phone in a bedroom or a school laptop, and the copy deserves the highest-contrast surface on the page. Energetic and workshop-bright rather than sleek – the promise is a soldering iron, not a SaaS trial.

Every outline is a drawn ink stroke rather than a rectangle: card borders wobble, the week arrives as a band of torn painted paper, and page titles hang from straps on torn plates. It reads as something kept by hand alongside the hardware, which is what journalling and timelapses actually are. Where the landing page is ink-grounded and engineered, the platform is paper-grounded and warm, and its structure is a path you walk rather than a page you read. Even the one screen that borrows a familiar layout – the Doomscroller's reel player – is drawn in the notebook's hand rather than as a dark cinema.

rules.body: A token from one world never appears in the other. If a platform screen needs an accent, it is sky, not hl-cyan. The two palettes do not share a single value, and a screen that mixes them belongs to neither.
rules.name: The Two Worlds Rule

rules.body: A surface is drawn in one kit, not a blend of both. When one component has to appear in both worlds it names the surface it is on and swaps its class set (see DisputeThread); it does not import the other world's primitives. The console's palette is a deliberate copy of the platform's rather than an alias of it, and src/app/components/ui/ops-tokens.test.ts fails if a shared hue drifts; the promotion strip's literal fallbacks are guarded the same way.
rules.name: The One Kit Per Surface Rule

rules.body: Secondary text is tinted from its own surface, never neutral grey. The landing derives hl-ink-soft as ink at 80% over paper and hl-paper-soft as paper at 78% over ink. The platform's secondary text is navy-soft, the navy hue lifted until it reads as a second voice.
rules.name: The Tinted Secondary Rule

rules.body: On the trail a puck's colour is its state, and each state owns one hue: sky open, teal done, magenta hand-in, gold setup, sand locked, teal-grey passed. Don't reuse these hues on a puck for anything else.
rules.name: The State Colour Rule

rules.body: --color-hl-yellow (#A2C4DA) and --color-hl-yellow-pale (#EBF7FF) are blue. The landing was recoloured after those variables were named and the names were never updated, so the carousel cards read as pale blue while the code says yellow. Trust the value, not the name – and rename them before adding anything new that uses them.
rules.name: The Misnamed Yellow Rule

rules.body: Each role above has one size on a screen. Five near-identical hand sizes (12.2, 12.8, 13.1, 13.4, 13.8px) read as untidiness, not hierarchy; asides are 0.84rem, body 0.9rem, timeline titles 0.95rem.
rules.name: The One Size Per Role Rule

rules.body: The platform's hand-lettered face sets labels, asides and nothing longer – never a requirement or an instruction someone has to read to finish a task. The comp names COMICO, which is not on Google Fonts and ships no licensed file here; Shantell Sans stands in, loaded in the platform root layout and reached everywhere through --font-hand. Swapping it is that one variable, because no component names a face directly.
rules.name: The Hand Is Not Body Rule

rules.body: On the landing, Masterpiece is identity, never voice. It sets the wordmark and nothing else – it ships one 400 weight whose strokes overhang their advances (I carries 0.52em of ink on a 0.32em advance), so it is already heavy and a synthesised bold smears it. font-synthesis-weight: none is set for that reason.
rules.name: The Brush Bookends Rule

rules.body: Ubuntu is not a drop-in for Open Sans. Against the same fallback reference Next scales Open Sans to 105.15% and Ubuntu to 102.06%, so Ubuntu sets about 3% smaller at the same font-size, and its declared ink box is 1.0984em against Open Sans's 1.2951em. Size the two independently.
rules.name: The Metric Drift Rule

rules.body: A panel, card, button or field is separated by an outline – drawn on the platform, a 2px rule in the staff console – and the page ground showing through, never by a shadow. If something needs separating, give it a border and a gap.
rules.name: The Outline-Not-Shadow Rule

rules.body: A shadow means an object sitting on the notebook – a puck, a sticker, a strip of tape, a reel. If it isn't something you could pick up, it doesn't get one.
rules.name: The Paper-On-Paper Rule

rules.body: A platform border is drawn, not stroked. Use .sketch (or .sketch-2 / .sketch-3, which carry different seeds) rather than a CSS border, and vary which one between adjacent cards. Two cards with the same wobble read as a repeated texture, which is the opposite of hand-made. The staff console is the exception: a panel, field or button there takes a real 2px border (ops-border, or field-edge on a field), and only the sign's plaque is torn.
rules.name: The Drawn Edge Rule

rules.body: The displacement filter goes on the border element only, never on a container. Filtering an element that holds text drags the text through the same displacement and turns it to mush.
rules.name: The Filter Applies To The Edge Rule

rules.body: .sketch draws on a pseudo-element, and <input>, <select> and <textarea> cannot hold one – the outline silently never renders and the field is a white box on a white panel. Fields take a real 2px border instead (see Inputs).
rules.name: The No Sketch On Fields Rule
